settler: Settlers were the families who left crowded homelands to break new ground, carrying seed, tools and livestock to an unclaimed valley or coast. In the game the Settler founds a new city or joins an existing one, adding its people. It costs two citizens of the city that trains it, cannot fight, and should travel with an escort wherever barbarians or rivals roam.
worker: Every road, field and mine in history was built by ordinary labourers with shovels, ploughs and oxen. Workers improve the land around your cities: they irrigate, mine, build roads and later railroads, clear forests and fight pollution. They cannot defend themselves, and an enemy who catches one alone takes it as a captive. See [Workers](pedia:concepts/workers) for job times.
scout: Scouts have run ahead of armies and caravans since the earliest times, reading the land and reporting what lay beyond the next hill. Only expansionist civilizations train them, and each starts the game with one, or with its own unique scout such as the Inca [Chasqui Scout](pedia:units/chasquiScout). The Scout moves quickly, cannot fight, and is ideal for finding tribal villages, rivals and good city sites early on. It upgrades to the [Explorer](pedia:units/explorer).
explorer: The age of discovery sent explorers deep into unmapped continents, often guided by local peoples along trails no outsider knew. The Explorer treats every tile as if it had a road, so it crosses jungles, mountains and marshes at full speed. It cannot fight, but it charts new lands, meets distant civilizations and finds the last tribal villages faster than anything else.
marine: Modern marines are trained to fight their way ashore from ships, seizing beaches and ports under fire. The Marine can attack directly from a ship at sea onto a land tile, so it can storm a coastal city without first landing beside it. It is strong on the attack but modest on defence, and needs Rubber to build. See [Naval units](pedia:concepts/naval).
modernParatrooper: Today's airborne forces combine parachute assault with heavy weapons and armoured vehicles dropped by air. The Modern Paratrooper can be airdropped from one of your cities onto distant ground, then holds what it seizes with a very solid defence. It is the final step of the airborne line, improving on the [Paratrooper](pedia:units/paratrooper).
warrior: The first warriors were hunters who turned their clubs and spears against rival bands. The Warrior is the cheapest military unit and the one every civilization can build from the start. It is weak at both attack and defence, but a single Warrior can guard a new city, escort a Settler or scout nearby lands. It upgrades to the [Swordsman](pedia:units/swordsman).
archer: The bow let ancient soldiers strike from a distance, and massed archers decided many early battles. The Archer is an early attacker, stronger than a Warrior on the offence and able to weaken a defender with a light ranged bombardment. Its defence is poor, so pair it with spearmen. It upgrades to the [Longbowman](pedia:units/longbowman).
spearman: Spearmen standing shoulder to shoulder formed the backbone of nearly every ancient army, holding the line against charging foes. The Spearman is the first true defender: cheap, sturdy behind walls, and enough to keep early raiders out of your cities. It can also be drafted. It upgrades to the [Pikeman](pedia:units/pikeman).
swordsman: Iron swords gave ancient infantry a weapon that was both strong and cheap to forge in numbers. The Swordsman is the main early attacker once you know [Iron Working](pedia:techs/ironWorking) and have access to Iron. It hits hard enough to take lightly defended cities but should not be left to defend them. It upgrades to Medieval Infantry.
chariot: Horse-drawn chariots carried archers and spearmen swiftly across open plains and ruled ancient battlefields for centuries. The Chariot is the first fast unit, moving two tiles a turn, but it is fragile and its wheels slow it in rough country. It needs Horses and upgrades to the [Horseman](pedia:units/horseman).
horseman: Riding astride horses gave early peoples speed for raiding, scouting and pursuit. The Horseman moves two tiles a turn and makes a good early raider and explorer, though its defence is weak. It needs Horses. Barbarians favour it once the world grows older. It upgrades to the [Knight](pedia:units/knight).
pikeman: Long pikes allowed medieval foot soldiers to stop a cavalry charge cold. The Pikeman is the medieval city defender, sturdier than the Spearman and especially effective against mounted attackers. It needs Iron, can be drafted, and upgrades to the [Musketman](pedia:units/musketman) once gunpowder arrives.
longbowman: The longbow, drawn with great strength, could pierce armour at long range and won famous victories in the hands of trained yeomen. The Longbowman is a medieval attacker that needs no strategic resource, which makes it valuable when Iron or Horses are scarce. It can also soften defenders with a ranged bombardment. It upgrades to the [Guerilla](pedia:units/guerilla).
musketman: Firearms changed warfare for good: a peasant with a musket could stand against a knight. The Musketman is the gunpowder-era defender, much tougher than the Pikeman, and needs Saltpeter. It can be drafted, holds cities for a long time, and upgrades to the [Rifleman](pedia:units/rifleman).
knight: Armoured knights on heavy warhorses were the elite of medieval warfare, bound to their lords by oaths of service. The Knight is a strong, fast attacker that also defends reasonably well, making it a good unit to lead medieval offensives. It needs both Horses and Iron, and upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
rifleman: Rifled barrels made infantry deadly accurate at long range, and national armies of riflemen filled the battlefields of the nineteenth century. The Rifleman is the defender of the industrial age, needs no strategic resource, and can be drafted. It holds cities well against cavalry and cannon. It upgrades to [Infantry](pedia:units/infantry).
cavalry: Light cavalry armed with sabres and carbines remained a fast striking force into the age of rifles. Cavalry moves three tiles a turn and hits hard, making it the best attacker before the age of tanks. It needs Horses and Saltpeter. It has no further upgrade, so plan to replace it with armour once [Tanks](pedia:units/tank) arrive.
infantry: The infantry of the world wars dug in behind trenches, machine guns and barbed wire, making defence stronger than ever before. Infantry is the main defender of the early modern era and needs Rubber. It can be drafted and upgrades to [Mech Infantry](pedia:units/mechInfantry).
tank: Armoured tracked vehicles broke the deadlock of trench warfare and became the spearhead of modern armies. The Tank attacks with great force and can make more than one attack per turn while it has movement left. It needs Oil and Rubber, and upgrades to [Modern Armor](pedia:units/modernArmor).
mechInfantry: Mechanized infantry ride into battle in armoured personnel carriers, combining mobility with the staying power of foot soldiers. Mech Infantry is the strongest defender in the game and moves two tiles a turn, so it can rush to threatened cities. It needs Oil and Rubber and can be drafted.
modernArmor: Today's main battle tanks carry composite armour, stabilised guns and advanced fire control. Modern Armor is the most powerful land attacker in the game, moving three tiles and able to attack several times per turn. It needs Oil, Rubber and Aluminum. Pair it with artillery and air power to break any defence.
catapult: Ancient engineers built catapults to hurl stones over and against city walls. The Catapult cannot attack in the normal way: it bombards units in an adjacent tile, wearing down defenders before your infantry strikes. It is defenceless and is captured if caught alone. See [Bombardment](pedia:concepts/bombard). It upgrades to the [Trebuchet](pedia:units/trebuchet).
cannon: Gunpowder artillery brought down castle walls that had stood for centuries. The Cannon bombards an adjacent tile, damaging defenders, city improvements or terrain improvements, and needs Iron and Saltpeter. Keep it stacked with defenders, since it cannot protect itself. It upgrades to [Artillery](pedia:units/artillery).
artillery: Industrial artillery fired explosive shells far beyond the line of sight, and dominated the battlefields of the world wars. Artillery bombards targets up to two tiles away, so it can strike without standing next to the enemy. It cannot defend itself and is best kept in a stack or city. It upgrades to [Radar Artillery](pedia:units/radarArtillery).
radarArtillery: Modern self-propelled guns use radar and computers to locate targets and fire with great precision. Radar Artillery bombards up to two tiles away with the heaviest punch of any ground gun, and moves two tiles a turn. It needs Aluminum. Like all artillery it relies on other units to protect it. See [Bombardment](pedia:concepts/bombard).
cruiseMissile: Cruise missiles are guided, pilotless weapons that skim low over land and sea to hit targets far away. In the game the Cruise Missile is a single-use weapon: it strikes a target within its range with a heavy bombardment that can destroy units outright, and is spent in the attack. It needs Aluminum and can be carried by ships.
tacticalNuke: Tactical nuclear weapons are smaller warheads intended for use on the battlefield rather than against whole nations. The Tactical Nuke strikes a target within range, destroying most units around it, damaging the city it hits and causing fallout. Using one angers the whole world. It needs Aluminum and Uranium. See [Nuclear weapons](pedia:concepts/nukes).
icbm: Intercontinental ballistic missiles can deliver a nuclear warhead to any point on the globe within minutes. The ICBM cannot move but can strike any tile on the map from the city where it waits, devastating the target area. It needs Aluminum and Uranium, and its use brings fallout and outrage. See [Nuclear weapons](pedia:concepts/nukes).
galley: Oared galleys carried trade and troops around the Mediterranean for thousands of years, rarely venturing far from shore. The Galley is the first transport ship, carrying two land units, but it is at risk of sinking anywhere beyond coastal waters. It upgrades to the [Caravel](pedia:units/caravel). See [Naval units](pedia:concepts/naval).
caravel: The nimble caravel, with its lateen sails, let Portuguese and Spanish sailors probe the coasts of Africa and cross the Atlantic. The Caravel carries three land units and can sail the open sea, though deep ocean is still dangerous. It is the ship of early exploration and colonization. It upgrades to the [Galleon](pedia:units/galleon).
frigate: Frigates were fast, well-armed sailing warships used for patrol, escort and raiding. The Frigate is the first real warship: it attacks enemy ships and can bombard coastal targets near it. It needs Iron and Saltpeter. It remains useful until steam-powered warships arrive.
galleon: Galleons were large, sturdy sailing ships that carried treasure and cargo across the oceans of the world. The Galleon is a transport that can cross any ocean safely, carrying four land units, but it is a poor fighter and should be escorted in wartime. It upgrades to the [Transport](pedia:units/transport).
ironclad: Ironclads were steam-powered warships armoured with iron plates, making wooden navies obsolete almost overnight. The Ironclad is a strong coastal warship that can attack and bombard nearby targets, and needs Iron and Coal. Its range at sea is limited compared with later ships. It upgrades to the [Destroyer](pedia:units/destroyer).
transport: Modern troop transports moved whole armies across the oceans to invade distant shores. The Transport carries six land units and moves quickly, but it is weak in battle and needs warships to protect it. It needs Oil. See [Naval units](pedia:concepts/naval).
carrier: Aircraft carriers are floating airbases that let a navy project air power anywhere in the world. The Carrier holds four aircraft, which can operate from it as if from a city, and it sees far with its radar. It is poorly armed, so escort it with destroyers and cruisers. It needs Oil. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
submarine: Submarines struck from beneath the waves and nearly strangled island nations in two world wars. The Submarine attacks with surprise and can pick its target, but it is fragile in a fight. In this game submarines are not hidden: every player sees them like any other ship. It needs Oil. Destroyers are its main threat.
destroyer: Destroyers are fast escort warships built to hunt submarines and screen larger ships. The Destroyer is quick, hunts submarines, bombards nearby targets and protects transports and carriers. It needs Oil. It is the workhorse warship of the modern era. See [Naval units](pedia:concepts/naval).
battleship: Battleships carried the largest guns and heaviest armour ever put to sea, and were long the measure of naval power. The Battleship is the strongest warship in a straight fight and can bombard coastal targets two tiles away, smashing defences before an invasion. It needs Oil.
aegisCruiser: AEGIS cruisers carry advanced radar and missile systems designed to defend a fleet against air and missile attack. The AEGIS Cruiser is a powerful modern warship that protects nearby units from aircraft and missiles. It needs Aluminum and Uranium, and improves on the [Cruiser](pedia:units/cruiser).
nuclearSubmarine: Nuclear-powered submarines can stay submerged for months and carry missiles that reach far inland. The Nuclear Submarine is visible like any other ship here, but it can carry a tactical missile to launch near an enemy coast. It needs Uranium. See [Nuclear weapons](pedia:concepts/nukes).
fighter: Fighter aircraft first fought for control of the skies over the trenches of the First World War. The Fighter intercepts enemy aircraft, attacks units and can sink ships with its bombing runs. It operates from cities and carriers within its operational range. It needs Oil and upgrades to the [Jet Fighter](pedia:units/jetFighter). See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
bomber: Heavy bombers carried the war to enemy factories, cities and supply lines. The Bomber cannot fight other aircraft but delivers a heavy bombardment that can destroy units on land and sea and wreck city improvements. It needs Oil and benefits from fighters clearing the skies first. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
helicopter: Helicopters can hover and land almost anywhere, carrying troops to places no road or runway reaches. The Helicopter is an air unit that carries up to three foot soldiers between cities and the field. It needs Oil and Rubber. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
jetFighter: Jet engines pushed fighters past the speed of sound and transformed air combat after the Second World War. The Jet Fighter is a faster, deadlier interceptor and strike aircraft than the propeller [Fighter](pedia:units/fighter), able to sink ships with its attacks. It needs Oil and Aluminum.
stealthFighter: Stealth aircraft use special shapes and coatings to slip past enemy radar. The Stealth Fighter is a versatile strike aircraft that is rarely intercepted, and its bombardment can destroy units on land or at sea. It needs Oil and Aluminum. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
stealthBomber: The stealth bomber combines intercontinental range with near-invisibility to radar. The Stealth Bomber delivers the heaviest conventional bombardment in the game, can single out a chosen unit in a stack, and is rarely intercepted. It needs Oil and Aluminum. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
leader: Great commanders inspire their soldiers to deeds that lesser officers could never ask of them. A Leader appears when one of your elite units wins a battle. It cannot fight, but in a city it can form an [Army](pedia:units/army) or rush the construction of an improvement or wonder. Protect it, as an enemy that reaches it will destroy it. See [Leaders](pedia:concepts/leaders).
army: History's great campaigns were won by forces that fought as a single body under one command. An Army is formed by a great leader and holds up to three land units, which fight one after another so the army is very hard to destroy. Armies can attack several times a turn and reveal the land around them. See [Armies](pedia:concepts/armies).
jaguarWarrior: The jaguar warriors were an elite order of Aztec soldiers, dressed in jaguar skins, who sought captives for sacrifice. The Aztecs field the Jaguar Warrior in place of the Warrior: it costs a little more but moves two tiles a turn, which makes it a fine early raider and explorer. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the Swordsman.
bowman: Babylonian archers, armed with powerful composite bows, protected the cities of Mesopotamia. Babylon fields the Bowman in place of the Archer: it attacks just as well but has a better defence, so it can hold a city as well as raid. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the Longbowman.
hoplite: Greek hoplites, citizen-soldiers with round shields and long spears, fought in the tightly packed phalanx. Greece fields the Hoplite in place of the Spearman, with a stronger defence that makes Greek cities hard to take early on. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Musketman](pedia:units/musketman).
impi: The impi were Zulu regiments, trained to run long distances and strike with short stabbing spears and great shields. The Zulus field the Impi in place of the Spearman: it defends the same but moves two tiles a turn, so it can rush to wherever it is needed. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the Musketman.
legionary: The Roman legionary was a disciplined professional soldier who built roads and camps as readily as he fought. Rome fields the Legionary in place of the Swordsman, with a better defence, so it can both attack and hold what it takes. It needs Iron. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to Medieval Infantry.
immortals: The Immortals were the Persian king's elite guard, said to be kept at a constant strength of ten thousand. Persia fields Immortals in place of the Swordsman, with a stronger attack that makes them some of the best early city-takers. They need Iron. Their first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). They upgrade to the Guerilla.
warChariot: Egyptian war chariots, light and fast, carried archers who harassed enemies from a distance. Egypt fields the War Chariot in place of the Chariot, with a stronger attack that makes it a real early threat. It needs Horses. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Knight](pedia:units/knight).
rider: Chinese heavy horsemen guarded the frontiers of the empire against nomad raiders. China fields the Rider in place of the Knight: it fights the same but moves three tiles a turn, allowing deep strikes and quick retreats. It needs Horses and Iron. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
mountedWarrior: After horses spread through North America, mounted warriors became skilled raiders and hunters. The Iroquois field the Mounted Warrior in place of the Horseman, with a stronger attack that makes it a dangerous early raider. It needs Horses. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Knight](pedia:units/knight).
musketeer: The French royal musketeers were an elite guard famed for their courage and their swordsmanship. France fields the Musketeer in place of the Musketman, with a stronger defence that makes French cities very hard to take. It needs Saltpeter. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Rifleman](pedia:units/rifleman).
samurai: The samurai were Japan's warrior class, skilled with sword and bow and bound by a strict code of loyalty. Japan fields the Samurai in place of the Knight: it fights on foot, needs only Iron rather than Horses, and defends better than a Knight. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
warElephant: War elephants terrified enemy troops and horses, and were prized by Indian rulers for centuries. India fields the War Elephant in place of the Knight, with the same strength but needing no strategic resource at all, so India can field strong attackers even without Horses or Iron. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
cossack: Cossacks were free horsemen of the steppe frontier who became Russia's renowned light cavalry. Russia fields the Cossack in place of Cavalry: it is a little dearer but can attack several times in a turn while it has movement left. It needs Horses and Saltpeter. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges).
panzer: German armoured divisions, the Panzers, led the fast-moving offensives of the Second World War. Germany fields the Panzer in place of the Tank: it moves three tiles a turn instead of two, reaching deep into enemy territory. It needs Oil and Rubber. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Modern Armor](pedia:units/modernArmor).
manOWar: The British ship of the line, with its rows of heavy guns, gave England command of the seas for generations. England fields the Man-O-War in place of the Frigate, with a much stronger attack and bombardment that let it dominate the oceans of its age. It needs Iron and Saltpeter. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges).
privateer: Privateers were privately owned ships licensed by a government to prey on enemy shipping, and often hard to tell from pirates. In this game the Privateer sails under its own flag: like any warship it attacks only civilizations you are at war with, as a cheap raider of enemy shipping. It needs Iron and Saltpeter. Its defence is weak, so strike and slip away.
keshik: The keshik were the Mongol khan's mounted guard, trained horse archers who could ride and shoot at full gallop. The Mongols field the Keshik in place of the Knight: it is cheaper and needs only Horses, though its defence is lower. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
conquistador: The Spanish conquistadors crossed oceans and overthrew great empires in the Americas with small, determined bands. Spain fields the Conquistador in place of the [Explorer](pedia:units/explorer): like the Explorer it treats every tile as a road, but it is also a real fighting unit. It needs Horses. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges).
berserk: Norse berserkers were warriors said to fight in a wild frenzy, heedless of wounds. Scandinavia fields the Berserk in place of the Longbowman, with a fearsome attack, and it can attack straight from a ship onto the shore, just as Viking raiders did. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Guerilla](pedia:units/guerilla).
sipahi: The sipahi were Ottoman cavalrymen granted land in return for military service. The Ottomans field the Sipahi in place of [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry), with a much stronger attack that makes it the deadliest horseman of its age. It needs Horses and Saltpeter. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges).
gallicSwordsman: Celtic warriors of Gaul fought with long iron swords and were famous for their swift, fierce charges. The Celts field the Gallic Swordsman in place of the Swordsman: it moves two tiles a turn, giving the Celts a fast early strike force. It needs Iron. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to Medieval Infantry.
ansarWarrior: The Ansar were the early supporters of the Prophet in Medina, and Arab horsemen carried the new faith across a vast region. Arabia fields the Ansar Warrior in place of the Knight: it is cheaper and moves three tiles a turn, though it defends less well. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Cavalry](pedia:units/cavalry).
numidianMercenary: Numidian soldiers from North Africa served Carthage as hired troops in its long wars with Rome. Carthage fields the Numidian Mercenary in place of the Spearman, stronger in both attack and defence, and it can be drafted. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Pikeman](pedia:units/pikeman).
hwacha: The hwach'a was a Korean cart that launched dozens of rocket-propelled arrows at once. Korea fields the Hwach'a in place of the Cannon: it needs only Saltpeter, not Iron, and its bombardment can destroy units outright on land and at sea. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to [Artillery](pedia:units/artillery).
medievalInfantry: Medieval foot soldiers, armed with swords, axes and maces, formed the bulk of armies when knights were few. Medieval Infantry is an attacker of the middle ages, a step up from the Swordsman, and needs Iron. It can be drafted. It upgrades to the [Guerilla](pedia:units/guerilla).
guerilla: Guerilla fighters wage war by ambush and raid, using local knowledge to wear down stronger armies. The Guerilla needs no strategic resource, which makes it valuable for nations cut off from Rubber or Oil, and it can strike from a distance with a light bombardment. It can be drafted and upgrades to [TOW Infantry](pedia:units/towInfantry).
princess: Royal heirs were often prizes in war, held as hostages or married off to seal alliances. The Princess is a special scenario unit that cannot be built and cannot move on its own. Scenarios use it as a person to rescue, capture or guard.
lincoln: Abraham Lincoln led the United States through its civil war, preserved the union and ended slavery. In regicide games he is America's king unit: if he is killed, America is out of the game and its cities surrender to his killer. He is a poor fighter, so keep him well protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
hammurabi: Hammurabi united Mesopotamia under Babylon and is remembered for his famous code of laws, carved in stone. In regicide games he is Babylon's king unit: if he falls, Babylon is out of the game and its cities surrender. Keep him behind strong walls and defenders. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
mao: Mao Zedong led the Communist revolution that founded the People's Republic of China and ruled it for decades. In regicide games he is China's king unit: if he is killed, China loses and its cities surrender to the victor. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
bismarck: Otto von Bismarck, the Prussian chancellor, united the German states into one empire through diplomacy and short, decisive wars. In regicide games he is Germany's king unit: if he falls, Germany is out of the game and its cities surrender. Keep him safe in a well-defended city. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
alexander: Alexander of Macedon conquered an empire stretching from Greece to India before his death at the age of thirty-two. In regicide games he is Greece's king unit: if he is killed, Greece loses and its cities surrender to his killer. Unlike his namesake, he should stay far from the front. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
caesar: Julius Caesar conquered Gaul, won a civil war and became dictator of Rome before his assassination. In regicide games he is Rome's king unit: if he falls, Rome is out of the game and its cities surrender. Guard him well. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
xerxes: Xerxes ruled the Persian Empire at its height and led a vast invasion of Greece. In regicide games he is Persia's king unit: if he is killed, Persia loses and its cities surrender to the victor. Keep him well protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
hiawatha: Hiawatha is remembered as a co-founder of the Iroquois Confederacy, which joined several nations under a common law of peace. In regicide games he is the Iroquois king unit: if he falls, the Iroquois are out of the game and their cities surrender. Keep him safe. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
shaka: Shaka built the Zulu kingdom into a powerful military state through new tactics and strict discipline. In regicide games he is the Zulus' king unit: if he is killed, the Zulus lose and their cities surrender to his killer. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
montezuma: Montezuma ruled the Aztec Empire at the height of its power, when Spanish conquistadors arrived. In regicide games he is the Aztecs' king unit: if he falls, the Aztecs are out of the game and their cities surrender. Keep him well defended. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
cleopatra: Cleopatra, the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt, sought to preserve her kingdom through alliances with Rome's most powerful men. In regicide games she is Egypt's king unit: if she is killed, Egypt loses and its cities surrender. Protect her carefully. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
elizabeth: Elizabeth I reigned over England during a golden age of exploration and theatre, and saw off the Spanish Armada. In regicide games she is England's king unit: if she falls, England is out of the game and its cities surrender. Keep her safe. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
catherine: Catherine the Great expanded the Russian Empire and championed the arts and learning of the Enlightenment. In regicide games she is Russia's king unit: if she is killed, Russia loses and its cities surrender to the victor. Guard her well. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
abu: Abu Bakr was a close companion of the Prophet and the first caliph, who held the young Muslim community together. In regicide games he is Arabia's king unit: if he falls, Arabia is out of the game and its cities surrender. Keep him protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
hannibal: Hannibal of Carthage marched an army with war elephants over the Alps and defeated Rome in its own heartland. In regicide games he is Carthage's king unit: if he is killed, Carthage loses and its cities surrender to his killer. Keep him away from danger. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
osman: Osman I founded the dynasty that grew from a small frontier state into the Ottoman Empire. In regicide games he is the Ottomans' king unit: if he falls, the Ottomans are out of the game and their cities surrender. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
temujin: Temujin, better known as Genghis Khan, united the Mongol tribes and began the largest land empire in history. In regicide games he is the Mongols' king unit: if he is killed, the Mongols lose and their cities surrender. Keep him safe. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
gandhi: Mohandas Gandhi led India's movement for independence through non-violent resistance. In regicide games he is India's king unit: if he falls, India is out of the game and its cities surrender to the victor. Protect him well. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
ragnar: Ragnar Lodbrok is a legendary Viking chieftain whose raids and sons appear throughout the Norse sagas. In regicide games he is Scandinavia's king unit: if he is killed, Scandinavia loses and its cities surrender. Keep him out of harm's way. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
brennus: Brennus was a Gallic chieftain who defeated a Roman army and sacked Rome itself. In regicide games he is the Celts' king unit: if he falls, the Celts are out of the game and their cities surrender. Guard him well. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
tokugawa: Tokugawa Ieyasu unified Japan after a century of civil war and founded the shogunate that ruled for over two hundred years. In regicide games he is Japan's king unit: if he is killed, Japan loses and its cities surrender. Keep him well protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
joanDarc: Joan of Arc, a peasant girl guided by visions, rallied French forces to lift the siege of Orleans. In regicide games she is France's king unit: if she falls, France is out of the game and its cities surrender to the victor. Keep her safe. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
wangKon: Wang Kon founded the Goryeo dynasty in the tenth century and reunited the Korean peninsula after a long period of division. In regicide games he is Korea's king unit: if he is killed, Korea loses and its cities surrender. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
isabella: Isabella of Castile united Spain with Ferdinand of Aragon and sponsored the voyages of Columbus. In regicide games she is Spain's king unit: if she falls, Spain is out of the game and its cities surrender. Keep her protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
enkiduWarrior: In the epic of Gilgamesh, Enkidu is the wild man who becomes the king's companion; the Sumerians themselves fought in close ranks with spears and shields. Sumeria fields the Enkidu Warrior in place of the Warrior, with a stronger defence that makes it a cheap early guard. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Pikeman](pedia:units/pikeman).
threeManChariot: Hittite chariots carried a driver, a warrior and a shield-bearer, making them heavier and sturdier than those of their rivals. The Hittites field the Three-Man Chariot in place of the Chariot, stronger in both attack and defence. It needs Horses. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Knight](pedia:units/knight).
mursilis: Mursili I was a Hittite king who led his armies as far as Babylon and sacked it. In regicide games he is the Hittites' king unit: if he is killed, the Hittites lose and their cities surrender. Keep him well defended. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
gilgamesh: Gilgamesh was a king of Uruk whose deeds became the world's oldest surviving epic. In regicide games he is Sumeria's king unit: if he falls, Sumeria is out of the game and its cities surrender. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
henry: Prince Henry the Navigator sponsored the Portuguese voyages that opened the age of discovery along the African coast. In regicide games he is Portugal's king unit: if he is killed, Portugal loses and its cities surrender. Keep him safe. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
carrack: The carrack was a large, sturdy ocean-going ship that carried Portuguese traders all the way to India and beyond. Portugal fields the Carrack in place of the Caravel: it attacks better and can cross deep ocean safely, giving Portugal a head start in exploration. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Galleon](pedia:units/galleon).
swissMercenary: Swiss pikemen were the most sought-after mercenaries of Renaissance Europe, famous for their discipline. The Netherlands field the Swiss Mercenary in place of the Pikeman, with a stronger defence that makes Dutch cities hard to crack. It needs Iron and can be drafted. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Rifleman](pedia:units/rifleman).
williamOfOrange: William of Orange led the Dutch revolt against Spanish rule and is honoured as the father of the Netherlands. In regicide games he is the Netherlands' king unit: if he falls, the Dutch are out of the game and their cities surrender. Keep him protected. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
trebuchet: The trebuchet used a heavy counterweight to fling massive stones against castle walls. It bombards an adjacent tile harder than the [Catapult](pedia:units/catapult), wearing down defenders and destroying improvements, but cannot protect itself. Keep it in a stack with defenders. It upgrades to the [Cannon](pedia:units/cannon).
pachacuti: Pachacuti transformed the Inca kingdom of Cusco into a vast empire along the Andes and rebuilt its capital. In regicide games he is the Inca king unit: if he is killed, the Inca lose and their cities surrender. Guard him closely. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
smokeJaguar: Smoke-Jaguar was a ruler of the Maya city of Copan, which grew powerful under his long reign. In regicide games he is the Maya king unit: if he falls, the Maya are out of the game and their cities surrender. Keep him well defended. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
theodora: Theodora rose from humble beginnings to become empress beside Justinian and a powerful voice in Byzantine politics. In regicide games she is the Byzantines' king unit: if she is killed, the Byzantines lose and their cities surrender. Protect her well. See [Victory](pedia:concepts/victory).
chasquiScout: The chasqui were relay runners who carried messages swiftly along the Inca road network. The Inca field the Chasqui Scout in place of the Scout and start the game with one: it moves just as fast but can fight a little, so it survives encounters that would doom a normal scout. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Explorer](pedia:units/explorer).
javelinThrower: Maya warriors hurled javelins with spear-throwers before closing in with clubs edged with obsidian. The Maya field the Javelin Thrower in place of the Archer: it defends better and makes a solid early guard as well as an attacker. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It upgrades to the [Longbowman](pedia:units/longbowman).
dromon: The Byzantine dromon was a fast war galley armed with siphons that sprayed Greek fire, a liquid that burned even on water. The Byzantines field the Dromon in place of the Galley: it attacks harder and its bombardment can sink ships outright. Like the Galley it carries two units and must stay near the coast. Its first victory can start a [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges).
cruiser: Cruisers were fast, well-armed warships, smaller than battleships, used for scouting, escort and raiding. The Cruiser is a strong modern warship with radar, able to bombard nearby targets. It needs Oil and upgrades to the [AEGIS Cruiser](pedia:units/aegisCruiser).
crusader: The crusaders were knights and soldiers who took up the cross for campaigns to the Holy Land. Crusaders cannot be trained; the [Knights Templar](pedia:buildings/knightsTemplar) wonder provides one every few turns. The Crusader is a strong medieval attacker that needs no resources and costs nothing to build, making it ideal for an early offensive.
ancientCavalry: Greek and Macedonian horsemen gave ancient armies speed and striking power on the flanks. Ancient Cavalry cannot be trained; the [Statue of Zeus](pedia:buildings/statueOfZeus) provides one every few turns. It is a fast, fairly strong early unit that needs no resources, good for raiding or reinforcing defences.
curragh: Curraghs were boats of hide stretched over wooden frames, used by Celtic peoples to fish and travel along rocky coasts. The Curragh is the earliest boat, cheap and available with the alphabet, but it carries no cargo and sinks if it strays from the coast. It is useful for exploring nearby shores. It upgrades to the [Galley](pedia:units/galley).
paratrooper: Paratroopers jump from aircraft to seize ground behind enemy lines, a tactic first used on a large scale in the Second World War. The Paratrooper can be airdropped from one of your cities onto a nearby tile and defends well once landed. It needs Oil and Rubber. It upgrades to the [Modern Paratrooper](pedia:units/modernParatrooper).
towInfantry: TOW infantry carry wire-guided anti-tank missiles that let small teams destroy armoured vehicles. TOW Infantry is a sturdy late-era foot soldier that needs no strategic resource, strong on defence and able to bombard nearby units. It can be drafted, making it a good defender for nations without Oil or Rubber.
flak: Anti-aircraft guns filled the skies with exploding shells to bring down enemy bombers. The Flak unit protects cities and stacks against air attack and is weak in other fights. It is the first dedicated air defence on land. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air). It upgrades to the [Mobile SAM](pedia:units/mobileSam).
mobileSam: Mobile surface-to-air missile batteries can drive with an army and shoot down aircraft at long range. The Mobile SAM defends cities and stacks against air attack and moves two tiles a turn, so it can follow your armour. It is a poor fighter against ground units. See [Air units](pedia:concepts/air).
f15: The twin-engined F-15 Eagle gave the United States an air-superiority fighter that went decades without losing a dogfight. Americans fly it in place of the [Jet Fighter](pedia:units/jetFighter): the same strength and range, and its first victory can start an American [golden age](pedia:concepts/goldenAges). It intercepts raiders, escorts bombers, bombs targets and flies reconnaissance from cities and carriers.
